decision: Projects call the conveyor's reusable workflows, pinned to a version; nothing is copied into them.
why: snapall and lab-agent carry about 500 lines of nearly identical workflow each; copies drift and fixes do not travel.
rejected: A template repository; copy-paste with care; composite actions alone (they cannot hold whole jobs).

decision: The extraction is proven by moving snapall and lab-agent onto the conveyor with byte-for-byte the same published repositories - same URLs, same keys.
why: An extraction that changes what users receive cannot be told from a regression.
rejected: Proving it on a new project first.

decision: 'Nothing changed for users' means the same addresses and key, every signature verifying, and the README's install line installing the new release - not byte-identical packages.
why: Arch packages built twice differ in their timestamps; the byte promise could not be kept and would test nothing a user meets.
rejected: Byte-for-byte identical repositories (the earlier wording of this decision).

decision: Each project keeps its own signing key for now; one key for the whole commons is considered later.
why: A single key would change the trust of every existing installation at once.
rejected: One organisation key from the start.

decision: A project describes its delivery in one small declaration file; the workflow inputs stay few.
why: Inputs grow without limit and are scattered across callers; a file is read, reviewed and checked like data.

decision: The conveyor's scripts live inside its workflows, not as files it fetches.
why: A called workflow does not know which version of itself was called, so fetched files could drift from the workflow; inline, they move together with the tag.
rejected: A scripts folder checked out at run time.

decision: Arch (pacman) and Alpine (apk, for postmarketOS) first, each with a signed repository.
why: These are what the lab, the desktops and the phone actually run.
rejected: Debian and RPM repositories first - installation on them stays verified, as today.

decision: The declaration is read by a typed Rust reader that refuses unknown fields, not by Python inside the workflows.
why: Shipped code that other projects call: with Python a misspelled field is silently replaced by a default - a bug Rust's types rule out by design. Asked by the author: no Python for new things.
rejected: Python's tomllib inline (the first version); a shell TOML parser.

decision: Cutting versions stays with each language's own tool (release-plz for Rust); the conveyor starts from a release tag.
why: Versioning is part of a project's own decisions and tooling.
